section.title: The First Journey: Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe
section.sectionRationale: The first journey continues through the cities of Lycaonia. At Iconium the gospel divides the city; at Lystra a lifelong cripple is healed, and the pagan crowd nearly worships Paul and Barnabas before turning to stone Paul instead. Yet the apostles return through the very cities that opposed them, strengthening the young churches and appointing elders, then report to Antioch that God has opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
section.thesis: The gospel advances through both wonder and violence: it is confused with pagan worship, opposed to the point of stoning, yet it presses on as the apostles plant and strengthen churches, teaching that we enter God's kingdom through many hardships, because God Himself has opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
section.frameNote: Four movements: bold preaching and division at Iconium; the healing at Lystra and the crowd's attempt to sacrifice to the apostles; the stoning of Paul; and the return journey strengthening disciples, appointing elders, and reporting the open door at Antioch.

units.label: Bold witness and division at Iconium

verses.text: At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went as usual into the Jewish synagogue, where they spoke so well that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
So Paul and Barnabas spent considerable time there, speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His {{charis|grace}} by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.
The people of the city were divided. Some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles.
But when the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them,
they found out about it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region,
where they continued to preach the gospel.

units.label: Healing at Lystra and misplaced worship

verses.text: In Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet, who was lame from birth and had never walked.
This man was listening to the words of Paul, who looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed.
In a loud voice Paul called out, “Stand up on your feet!” And the man jumped up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have come down to us in human form!”
Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul they called Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, hoping to offer a sacrifice along with the crowds.

units.label: Turn from idols to the living God
units.note: we are only men; turn to the living God

verses.text: But when the {{apostoloi|apostles}} Barnabas and Paul found out about this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting,

“Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.
In past generations, He let all nations go their own way.
Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”
Even with these words, Paul and Barnabas could hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them.

units.label: The stoning of Paul
units.note: worshiped one hour, stoned the next

verses.text: Then some Jews arrived from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead.
But after the disciples had gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.

units.label: Strengthening the churches, the open door
units.note: many hardships, appointed elders, faith opened to the Gentiles

verses.text: They preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith. “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said.
Paul and Barnabas appointed {{presbyteroi|elders}} for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrusted them to the Lord, in whom they had believed.
After passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From Attalia they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work they had just completed.
When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they spent a long time there with the disciples.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favour. The Lord confirms the message of His grace with signs and wonders; the good news the apostles preach is a word of grace, and it is to God's grace that the whole work is finally commended, verse 26.

apostoloi.gloss: One sent, an emissary, an apostle. Luke calls Barnabas and Paul apostles, sent ones, here in the plural. They refuse the worship the crowd offers and insist they are only men, sent to point away from themselves to the living God.

presbyteroi.gloss: Elder, an appointed overseer of a local church. The apostles appoint elders in every young congregation, entrusting the churches to God through ordained leaders, so that the work would be established and continue after they moved on.

basic.context: Paul and Barnabas press on through the cities of Lycaonia. At Iconium their bold preaching wins many but splits the city, and a plot to stone them drives them to Lystra and Derbe. In Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the pagan crowd, thinking the gods have come down, tries to sacrifice to them as Zeus and Hermes. The apostles are horrified and beg the people to turn from idols to the living God. Then, stirred by opponents, the same kind of crowd stones Paul and leaves him for dead, yet he rises and continues. On the way home the two return through the hostile cities to strengthen the disciples and appoint elders, and report to Antioch that God has opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
basic.hermeneutics: Watch how quickly the crowd swings from worship to violence, a warning against building faith on signs and popularity. Note Paul's approach to pure pagans in verses 15 to 17: with no shared Scripture, he appeals to creation and God's kindness in rain and harvest as a bridge to the gospel. And hear the sober realism of verse 22, that the road into the kingdom runs through many hardships, set against the triumphant note that God has opened the door.
basic.originalLanguages: Three words frame the chapter. The Lord confirms the message of His grace, charis, with signs, and the whole work is commended to God's grace. Barnabas and Paul are named apostoloi, sent ones, who refuse worship and point to God. And they appoint presbyteroi, elders, in each church, planting leadership so the young congregations will endure.
basic.typology: Paul's appeal to the living God who made heaven and earth echoes the prophets' mockery of idols and Israel's confession of the one Creator. The healing of the man lame from birth recalls the sign at the temple gate in Acts 3 and points to the wholeness Christ brings, a foretaste of the restored creation.
basic.christ: Though Christ is not named in the speech to the pagans, He is the good news the apostles bring and the Lord who confirms the word of His grace. The apostles refuse the worship due to God alone, unlike the false gods of the crowd, and unlike Herod in the previous chapter. The kingdom they preach is Christ's kingdom, entered through the same path of suffering their Master walked.
basic.god: God is the living Creator who made heaven, earth, and sea, who has never left Himself without witness, giving rain and fruitful seasons even to nations that ignored Him. He is the one who opens the door of faith to the Gentiles and to whom the whole work is entrusted. Salvation is His doing from beginning to end.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 3 records a parallel healing of a man lame from birth. Romans 1 speaks of God's testimony in creation. Acts 10 shows God first opening the door to the Gentiles through Peter. Second Timothy 3 echoes that all who live godly in Christ will face persecution, the many hardships of verse 22.
basic.oneStory: The chapter carries the mission forward: the ascended Christ, by His Spirit and grace, plants churches among the Gentiles, and the door of faith swings open to the nations. The apostles do not merely win converts; they establish congregations with elders, so the word will take root and keep spreading toward the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Acts 14 has two parts of unequal weight. Verses 1 to 7 at Iconium repeat the pattern of Pisidian Antioch in short form, with preaching, belief, opposition, a divided city and a flight. Verses 8 to 20 at Lystra are the centre of the chapter, and verses 21 to 28 are the return journey, which Luke tells with a different tempo, city by city, in reverse order. The outward journey was a story of speeches and escapes; the homeward journey is a story of pastoral care.

The Lystra scene is built to echo the book's first healing. In Acts 3 Peter looks directly at a man lame from birth, says a command, and the man leaps up and walks. In Acts 14 Paul looks intently at a man lame from birth, sees his faith, calls out, and the man leaps up and walks. Luke is making a quiet point: Paul's ministry has the same marks as Peter's, and the same Lord is at work in both. In both cases the miracle is followed by a crowd, but where Peter in chapter 3 uses the crowd to preach Jesus, Paul in chapter 14 has first to stop the crowd from worshipping him.

The chapter is a story of two reversals. At Lystra the crowd move from worship to violence in a few verses, and Luke notes who made the difference: Jews who had come from Antioch and Iconium, verse 19. The reversal has a deeper irony, since Saul had stood by approving when Stephen was stoned, Acts 7:58, and now it is Paul who is dragged outside a city and stoned. Luke does not comment on it, but he does not need to.

The speech of verses 15 to 17 is one of the shortest speeches recorded in Acts, three verses long, and it is built on three questions it silently answers: who are we, what are you doing, and who is God. It has no quotation from Scripture, because the hearers have none. It is Luke's sketch of how to open a conversation with people who do not know the Bible.

The chapter's two final verses show a church that reports to its sender. The journey ends at the place where it began, with grace, verse 26, and with a gathered assembly, verse 27.
context.historical:
Iconium, Lystra and Derbe lay in the southern part of the Roman province of Galatia, in a region historically called Lycaonia, on the high plain of Asia Minor. Iconium was the most important of the three, on the main road. Lystra was a Roman colony, settled by Augustus as a military outpost, yet its people still spoke their own Lycaonian language, which Luke records in verse 11 and which explains why Paul and Barnabas did not understand what the crowd said until they saw the bulls and the garlands. Derbe lay further east and was the last stop before the return. Many scholars think these congregations are the 'churches of Galatia' to whom Paul later wrote his letter, though others place the letter's readers further north.

The crowd's reaction was shaped by local legend. The Roman poet Ovid tells a tale, set in the hill country of Phrygia, in which Zeus and Hermes visited a village in disguise. Only an old couple, Philemon and Baucis, took them in, and everyone else was destroyed. A people raised on this story would be anxious not to turn away the gods a second time. That explains both the speed of their conclusion and the readiness of the priest of Zeus, whose temple stood in front of the city, to bring bulls and garlands. Barnabas, named first, they took for Zeus, the chief god, while Paul, the chief speaker, was Hermes, the messenger god.

Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy under the law, and also the way a mob might kill. Paul later lists being stoned once among his hardships, 2 Corinthians 11:25, and reminds Timothy of what happened at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, 2 Timothy 3:10 to 11. Timothy was from Lystra, Acts 16:1, and Some have wondered whether he was among the disciples who gathered around Paul, but Luke does not say.

The appointment of elders matches the practice of Jewish synagogues and of the Jerusalem church, which already had elders, Acts 11:30. The journey home goes by sea from Attalia to Syrian Antioch, where the missionaries spend a long time with the disciples. This pause sets the stage for the dispute of chapter 15, since the men from Judea who unsettle the church will arrive at an Antioch that has just heard what God had done.
context.canonical:
The healing at Lystra picks up the Isaiah promise that 'the lame will leap like a deer', Isaiah 35:6, and Jesus cited the lame walking as a sign of the kingdom in Luke 7:22. The healed man 'jumped up' in verse 10, as the lame man in Acts 3 had been 'walking and leaping and praising God', Acts 3:8. The sign belongs to a chain of signs that begins with Jesus and continues through His apostles.

Paul's speech belongs to a short series of addresses to Gentiles in Acts. Here he starts from creation and provision. In Athens, Acts 17:22 to 31, he again starts with the Creator and says that God has set the bounds of nations so that they would seek Him. Romans 1:18 to 21 explains the principle behind both: God's power and nature can be seen from what He has made, so that people are without excuse. The phrase 'heaven and earth and sea and everything in them' is taken from the commandment about the Sabbath, Exodus 20:11, and the praise of Psalm 146:6, and the church used it in prayer in Acts 4:24. The Lystra crowd hears the language of Israel's creed addressed to people who had never heard it.

The provision of rain and fruitful seasons echoes the covenant promises of rain in its season, Leviticus 26:4 and Deuteronomy 11:14, and the prophets' reproach of a people who did not fear the LORD who gives the rains, Jeremiah 5:24. Paul says that what Israel knew as covenant blessing is available as a witness even to the nations. Jesus said the same of the Father's sun and rain on the evil and the good, Matthew 5:45.

The apostles' refusal of worship has a pair in Acts 10:25 to 26, where Peter lifts Cornelius from his knees, and a later one in Revelation 19:10, where an angel does the same to John. The hardships of verse 22 are repeated in Paul's reminders to Timothy, 2 Timothy 3:11, and in the stoned of Hebrews 11:37. And the open door of verse 27 is a metaphor Paul uses often, 1 Corinthians 16:9, 2 Corinthians 2:12 and Colossians 4:3, and one that the risen Christ applies to Himself in Revelation 3:7 to 8.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is addressing a church that has begun to wonder whether the Gentile mission is worth its price. The chapter's answer is to show both the price and the reward in one piece. A man is stoned, and a few verses later the same man is back in the city. Whole towns turn against the apostles, and in the same journey they appoint elders in each church. The door is open, and it is also a hard road.

He also intends the Lystra scene as a lesson in how to speak. The apostles do not accept the praise offered, and they do not start with the Jewish Scriptures. They begin with something every person has experienced, rain, harvest, food and gladness, and they say that those things have a Giver. Luke's readers, many of them Gentiles, would have known what it was to be addressed in this way.

The closing verses show Luke's concern that the work is God's and the church's. The missionaries are 'commended to the grace of God' on departure and report 'all that God had done with them' on return. The glory is never theirs. What began as an act of the church at Antioch ends as a report to the church at Antioch, so the whole journey is shown as the church's ministry and God's work at once.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a miracle, a riot, a stoning and an appointment, and none of these is commanded as a pattern. Luke does not say that every preacher must expect to be stoned or that every church must be founded by a journey like this one. Nor does he say that those in need of healing will be healed when someone looks at them with attention. The details of the Lystra scene, the bulls and wreaths and the Lycaonian cry, belong to that place and moment.

The prescriptive weight lies in what is plainly taught and commended. Verse 22 contains the only direct statement of the chapter: 'We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.' It is a teaching given to new believers, and it carries authority because it is taught by apostles in the course of establishing churches. Equally clear is the practice of appointing elders in each church with prayer and fasting and entrusting them to the Lord. The Pastoral Letters confirm it, Titus 1:5. The refusal of worship is also a standing example: no servant of Christ may take for himself what is God's.

The approach to the pagan crowd is descriptive, but it matches Paul's later practice at Athens and the pattern of Romans 1. It may be treated as a wise example, not a fixed formula. The same man who spoke only of the Creator at Lystra spoke of Christ crucified elsewhere, and neither is the whole of his method.

debates.question: How should the church witness to people with no knowledge of Scripture, as at Lystra?

views.label: Begin with the Creator and His kindness
views.case: The strongest case follows Paul's own method: with pagans who share no Bible, he starts from creation and God's goodness in rain and harvest, common ground that exposes the folly of idols and points to the living God. This does not replace the gospel but builds a bridge to it, as Paul does again at Athens.

views.label: Preach Christ crucified directly
views.case: Others stress that the message of salvation is Christ and His cross, and that appeals to creation are only a preface that must quickly give way to the specific good news of Jesus. Rightly held, this guards against a natural theology that never reaches the Savior, though Paul shows the preface itself is a legitimate and wise first step.

debates.bearing: Held together, the passage teaches a witness that meets people where they are, from creation to Christ, without ever stopping short of the crucified and risen Lord who alone saves.

debates.question: Who appointed the elders, verse 23, and how?

views.label: The apostles appointed them
views.case: The subject of the sentence is Paul and Barnabas, and Titus 1:5 shows an apostle's delegate appointing elders in every town. On this reading the verb means simply to appoint, and the apostles chose the men, with prayer and fasting, as those with authority to plant churches.

views.label: The congregations chose them with the apostles' guidance
views.case: The verb Luke uses originally meant to stretch out the hand, as in a vote. The only other use in the New Testament is in 2 Corinthians 8:19, where a brother was 'chosen by the churches'. Some therefore think the churches had a voice, as the whole group did in choosing the seven in Acts 6:5 to 6, even though the apostles led and confirmed.

debates.bearing: The verb may by this time have meant simply to appoint, so it cannot decide the matter alone. What is clear is that leadership was in place from the start, was received with prayer, and was not left to chance.

debates.question: In what sense are Barnabas and Paul called apostles, verses 4 and 14?

views.label: Missionaries sent out by the church at Antioch
views.case: Luke has just told how the church at Antioch laid hands on them and sent them out, 13:3. The word apostle simply means sent one, and Paul uses it elsewhere of messengers from the churches, 2 Corinthians 8:23. On this view Luke is calling them sent ones of the church, without placing them among the Twelve.

views.label: Apostles of Christ in the full sense
views.case: Paul insists that he is an apostle not from men but from Jesus Christ, Galatians 1:1, and he lists Barnabas with himself in 1 Corinthians 9:5 to 6 as one with a right to support. Some think Luke here uses the word in the wider sense that includes Paul's commissioning by the risen Lord, and Barnabas as a recognised companion.

debates.bearing: Luke uses the word of both men only in this chapter, and the point of the scene is their refusal of worship, so the question of rank is less important to him than the question of whom they point to.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the speech and the strange idea of 'bearing witness' in verse 3. The Lord, Luke says, was 'testifying' to the word of His grace, martyreo, by giving signs and wonders. The signs are God's testimony, not the apostles' credentials. The same root will give us the word martyr, and in this chapter it is the apostles who risk a martyr's end, while God is the one who bears witness. When we reach verse 17 the idea returns. God, Paul says, did not leave Himself 'without testimony', using a double negative that puts the matter in the mildest form. The ordinary gifts of rain and harvest are His witness among the nations.

The man at Lystra had 'faith to be healed', verse 9. The verb is sozo, the ordinary New Testament word for to save and also for to make well. Luke chose it deliberately. The man hears Paul speak, hears the good news, and believes it, and the healing is the visible form of a salvation that reaches the whole person. The same word is used for the lame man's healing in Acts 4:9 and for the salvation Peter announces in Acts 4:12.

The cry of the crowd is in 'the Lycaonian language', a word that appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Luke explains why the apostles reacted so late, and he shows that he knows the region.

The priest brought bulls and wreaths to the 'gates', the Greek word pylon. In Acts 12:13 the same word means the gateway of Mary's house, where Rhoda failed to open it. Here it may be the gate of the city, as the BSB reads, or the gate of the house where the apostles lodged. Either way the sacrifice is stopped at the doorstep.

In verse 14 the apostles 'tore their clothes'. It is the gesture of horror at blasphemy, as the high priest did at the trial of Jesus, Mark 14:63. To be worshipped as a god was to them what saying Jesus was a blasphemer was to the Sanhedrin.

The central plea of verse 15 is that they are 'human like you'. The Greek word, homoiopathes, means of like nature and feelings, and the only other place it appears in the New Testament is James 5:17, where Elijah, who prayed that it would not rain, is called 'a man just like us'. A wonder-worker is still a man. The 'worthless things', mataia, are the Old Testament's word for idols, as in 2 Kings 17:15, where they pursued worthless idols and became worthless. Paul describes the turning as a turn 'to the living God', which Paul later describes in 1 Thessalonians 1:9 as turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God.

Verse 16 says God 'let all nations go their own way'. The verb means to permit and does not mean to approve. It is related to the later statement that He 'overlooked' the ignorance of earlier times, Acts 17:30, and is quite different from the 'gave them over' of Romans 1:24, which describes judicial abandonment. Paul's point here is patience.

Finally, the word for 'entrusted' in verse 23, paratithemai, is a banking term for placing a deposit with someone for safe keeping. The apostles deposit the churches with the Lord, and Paul will speak the same way to the Ephesian elders, Acts 20:32. The word for 'strengthening' in verse 22, sterizo, means to make firm, and the word for 'door' in verse 27, thyra, appears in the passages in which Paul speaks of open doors for the word.

typology.type: The lame man who leaps, Isaiah 35:6
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foretold that when God came to save, 'the lame will leap like a deer', and Jesus answered John's question about whether He was the one to come by pointing to the lame who walk, Luke 7:22. The man at Lystra, lame from birth, jumps up and walks at Paul's word. The healing is a down payment of the world the prophets promised, in which streams in the desert accompany the leaping of the lame. The escalation comes in Christ's own resurrection and the resurrection of the body promised to believers, in which no one will limp again. The type falls short because the healed man will one day die, and his legs are a sign of the kingdom and not the kingdom itself.

typology.type: The apostle stoned and walking back into the city
typology.fulfillment: Jesus told His disciples, 'No servant is greater than his master. If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well,' John 15:20. Those who took up stones against Jesus, John 8:59 and 10:31, were not done, and at Lystra the stones fall on His servant. Paul later says he carries about in his body 'the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed', 2 Corinthians 4:10. Paul's rising and re-entering the city is a pattern of the way suffering does not end the witness. It is not a resurrection, since Luke says he was presumed dead, and it falls short of the cross, since Paul's suffering is not atoning. It teaches the shape of a life that follows Christ.

typology.type: Elders appointed to share the shepherding, Exodus 18 and Numbers 11
typology.fulfillment: Moses was told to choose capable, God-fearing men to share the load of judging, Exodus 18:21 to 22, and later seventy elders were given a share of the Spirit that rested on him, Numbers 11:16 to 17. Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in each church so the burden of care is shared and the work does not hang on two travellers. The pattern escalates in Christ the Chief Shepherd, whose under-shepherds are told to shepherd God's flock willingly, not lording it over them, 1 Peter 5:1 to 4. It falls short in that no human elder can bear the weight of the flock; they are accountable to the Chief Shepherd and not substitutes for Him.

typology.type: God's gifts of rain and harvest as a witness that points beyond themselves
typology.fulfillment: Under the covenant, rain in season was the promised sign of the LORD's blessing, Leviticus 26:4 and Deuteronomy 11:14. Paul claims that the same gifts have been given to all nations as a standing witness. In Christ the pattern reaches its centre, for the Father who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good, Matthew 5:45, sent His Son to give life to the world, and the bread that the Father provides is Christ Himself, John 6:35. The pattern falls short in that common kindness leads toward repentance, Romans 2:4, but cannot save by itself.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in the speech at Lystra, and it would be a mistake to read Him into it. But the chapter leads to Him in several ways that the text and the New Testament make plain.

It leads to Christ by contrast with Herod and with the Lystran crowd. When the people try to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas, they tear their clothes and refuse. No one who bears the Lord's name can accept worship. Yet Jesus does accept it. The disciples in the boat worship Him and say, 'Truly You are the Son of God,' Matthew 14:33. The women grasp His feet and worship Him, Matthew 28:9, and the man born blind, once healed, says 'Lord, I believe' and worships Him, John 9:38. The writer to the Hebrews cites the Father's command, 'Let all God's angels worship Him,' Hebrews 1:6. The apostles refuse what Jesus receives, and the difference tells us who He is.

It leads to Christ in the sign. The man lame from birth is healed by the word of a man who looks at him and sees faith. The kingdom that Isaiah described, in which the lame leap, is what Jesus brought and said He brought, Luke 7:22. The apostles carry on in His name what He began, and in Acts 3 and 4 Peter said it plainly: the healing is by the name of Jesus Christ.

It leads to Christ in the path. The apostles say that it is necessary to endure many hardships to enter the kingdom, and the verb is the same word of divine necessity that Jesus used on the road to Emmaus: 'Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?' Luke 24:26. The disciple's road is shaped by the Master's. Jesus had said that a servant is not greater than his master, John 15:20, and Paul at Lystra is a living example.

It leads to Christ in the door and in the entrusting. The churches are entrusted to 'the Lord in whom they had believed', verse 23, which is a reference to Jesus. The door of faith that God opened to the Gentiles has a keeper: He is the one who 'holds the key of David' and what He opens no one can shut, Revelation 3:7. He also said, 'I am the gate,' John 10:9. The elders are shepherds under Him, and when the Chief Shepherd appears they will receive the crown, 1 Peter 5:4.

As always, take care with details. The stones are not a type of the cross, and Lystra is not Golgotha. The links given here are those that Jesus Himself and the apostles state.
study.god:
The Lystra speech is the fullest portrait in Acts of what a Gentile should hear first about God, and it holds three claims together. He is the living God, in contrast to the 'worthless things' the crowd was about to honour. He is the Creator, 'who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them', the same words the church had prayed in Acts 4:24. And He is the God who gives. Rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food and gladness are not accidents of nature but gifts from a hand.

That last point deserves a pause. Paul says that God fills the hearts of the people with 'food and gladness'. God is not a distant maker who set the world running, and He is not a stingy master who gives the least He can. He intends gladness, as the psalmist knew when he said that God had put more joy in his heart than when grain and new wine abound, Psalm 4:7. The gratitude that should have followed, as Romans 1:21 says, did not. People took the gifts and forgot the Giver. The apostles' task is to give the gifts back their address.

He is patient. 'In past generations, He let all nations go their own way.' This is not indifference, since the next phrase shows that He kept a witness. It is the patience that Paul says elsewhere is meant to lead to repentance, Romans 2:4, and that in Athens becomes the statement that God overlooked earlier ignorance but now commands all to repent, Acts 17:30. The God of Lystra has been giving rain to people who worshipped other gods, and He has been doing it for generations.

He is jealous for His glory. The apostles will not take what is His, and their horror is not modesty but theology. The living God will not share His worship, as Isaiah 42:8 says and as Herod found in the previous chapter.

He is the God who works with His servants. At the end of the chapter, the missionaries report 'all that God had done with them'. The preposition is with, not through, which allows both the divine initiative and human participation to stand. They did the work, and it was His. He opens the door, and they walk through it. He also does not remove the cost. The same God who heals the lame man and opens the door lets Paul be stoned, and the apostles say that the road to His kingdom runs through many hardships. Yet He rescues, as Paul says of these very places in 2 Timothy 3:11, 'the Lord rescued me from all of them'.

For worship, the chapter calls us to receive every good gift as a witness, to be glad before the Giver, and to give the glory away. A church that is wary of both self-importance and despair will find its model in a pair of tired men who tore their clothes rather than let a crowd call them gods, and who, a few days later, got up from the dust and went on to Derbe.

crossReferences.note: Peter looks directly at a man lame from birth, commands him to walk, and the man leaps up. Luke tells Paul's Lystra healing in the same beats, as if to say the same Lord who worked through Peter is working through Paul. The difference is in the crowd, who in Acts 3 gather to listen and in Acts 14 gather to worship.

Cornelius falls at Peter's feet to worship him, and Peter lifts him up and says he is only a man. The apostles at Lystra do the same with more drama, tearing their clothes, and the pair show the consistent apostolic refusal of what belongs to God alone.

Paul at Athens again begins with the God who made the world and gave life and breath to all, and speaks of the times of ignorance. The Athens speech is the fuller version of what Luke sketches at Lystra, with the same approach to people who have no Bible.

Paul explains why the argument from creation works: God's eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen from what He made, so that people are without excuse. The Lystra speech applies this to a crowd about to sacrifice to men.
Paul praises the Thessalonians for turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God. It is the same turning urged at Lystra, and shows what the apostles hoped a pagan crowd would do.

The promise that when God comes to save, the lame will leap like a deer and the mute will shout. The man at Lystra jumps up and walks, and the healing is a small fulfilment of what the prophet pictured for the whole creation.

The prophet reproaches a people who did not say in their hearts, Let us fear the LORD who gives the rains in season. Paul's claim that God gives rain and fruitful seasons assumes this old charge and extends it to every nation.

Stephen is dragged out of the city and stoned while Saul approves. At Lystra the stones fall on Paul, and he is dragged outside the city and left for dead. Luke leaves the connection to the reader, and it shows how grace has reshaped a persecutor.

Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions he suffered at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and says the Lord rescued him from them all. It confirms the stoning and shows that Timothy knew the story from his own home town.

On the Emmaus road Jesus says the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory. The apostles' word that believers must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom uses the same sense of necessity, so the way of the Master is set before the disciples.

Elders are told to shepherd God's flock willingly, as examples, and are promised a crown when the Chief Shepherd appears. This is the character of the leaders Paul and Barnabas appoint in verse 23 and the standard they would be judged by.

The risen Christ, who holds the key of David, says He has set an open door before the church at Philadelphia that no one can shut. It applies to Him the image Luke uses in verse 27 and shows who stands behind the open door of faith.

An angel with the eternal gospel calls every nation to fear God and worship the One who made the heavens, the earth and the sea. It is the Lystra message at its worldwide end, the same call to turn from worthless things to the Creator.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a God who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them, and who gave humanity a world full of food and gladness. Genesis 1 and 2 are the first of the gifts that Paul lists at Lystra, rain, fruitful seasons, food and joy. Then the story turns: humanity takes the gifts and forgets the Giver, builds towers, scatters, and takes up other gods. Paul's sentence, 'in past generations, He let all nations go their own way', is a summary of the history from Babel to the Roman Empire in a single line, and it is a generous one, for it says that God kept giving.

The call of Abraham in Genesis 12 begins the answer, and the long story of Israel is the way the answer takes form. Israel was meant to be the people through whom the nations would come to know the living God. When Paul stands among people who had never heard of Israel and says 'turn to the living God', he is doing what Israel had been called to do and had seldom done. The creed of Israel, that the LORD made the heavens, the earth and the sea, is for the first time spoken in a Lycaonian field to an audience who had no idea it existed.

The chapter also takes part in the story of the cost. The prophets suffered, Jesus suffered, Stephen suffered, and now Paul is dragged out of a city. The words 'many hardships' are not an accident of the first century. They are the shape of the age between Christ's rising and His return, and the churches that Paul and Barnabas strengthen are being prepared for it. Yet the same verse, verse 22, holds the goal, the kingdom of God, and the same chapter holds the word of an open door.

What the chapter sets up is the question of chapter 15. If the door of faith has been opened to the Gentiles, on what terms do they come in? The report that closes chapter 14 is the evidence the council will weigh, and the elders appointed in each church will be among those who live with the answer.

The story ends in the new creation, where the call that Paul gave at Lystra is answered at last. An angel flying overhead with the eternal gospel calls every nation to worship the One who made the heavens, the earth and the sea, Revelation 14:6 to 7, and the gathered multitude from every nation stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The lame will leap, the creation will be restored, and the gifts of the Giver will no longer be mistaken for anything else.

quiz.q: How did the crowd at Lystra react to the healing of the lame man?

options.text: They thought the gods had come down and tried to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13 show them calling the apostles Zeus and Hermes and preparing sacrifice.

options.text: They were amazed and wanted to make the apostles their leaders.
options.note: They were amazed, but specifically they tried to worship them as gods, which is the sharp point.

options.text: They quietly believed the gospel without any confusion.
options.note: There was great confusion; they misread the miracle as a visitation of pagan gods.

options.text: They ignored the miracle entirely.
options.note: Far from ignoring it, they were roused to attempt worship and sacrifice.

quiz.q: How did Paul and Barnabas respond to being treated as gods?

options.text: They tore their clothes and urged the crowd to turn from idols to the living God.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 record their horror and their redirection to the Creator.

options.text: They refused the worship and explained they were only men.
options.note: True, but it leaves out their positive call to turn to the living God who made all things.

options.text: They accepted the honour to gain a hearing for the gospel.
options.note: They did the opposite; they refused all such honour as belonging to God alone.

options.text: They welcomed the sacrifice as a sign of success.
options.note: They were appalled and rushed to stop it.

quiz.q: How did Paul preach to the pagan crowd who had no Scripture?

options.text: He appealed to the living God the Creator, who gives rain and harvest as a witness to His goodness.
options.note: Verses 15 to 17 build from creation and providence toward the true God.

options.text: He told them to abandon their idols as worthless things.
options.note: He did call them from worthless idols, but the heart of the appeal was the positive witness of the Creator's kindness.

options.text: He quoted the Law and the Prophets at length.
options.note: With pagans who lacked the Scriptures he appealed to creation, not to texts they did not know.

options.text: He offered no reason at all, only commands.
options.note: He gave clear reasons drawn from creation and God's providential goodness.

quiz.q: What did Paul and Barnabas do on the return journey?

options.text: They strengthened the disciples and appointed elders in each church.
options.note: Verses 22 to 23 show them establishing the churches for the long term.

options.text: They encouraged the disciples to continue in the faith through hardships.
options.note: True, but it omits the appointing of elders that secured each church's future.

options.text: They avoided the hostile cities to stay safe.
options.note: Remarkably, they returned through the very cities that had opposed them.

options.text: They abandoned the new believers and sailed home.
options.note: They did the opposite, revisiting and consolidating every young church.

quiz.q: What did the apostles report when they reached Antioch?

options.text: That God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
options.note: Verse 27 gives the summary: God Himself opened the Gentile door.

options.text: That they had made many disciples on the journey.
options.note: They did make disciples, but the reported climax is that God opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.

options.text: That the mission had been mostly a failure.
options.note: The report is of God's success in opening the door, not of failure.

options.text: That the Gentiles could not be reached.
options.note: The opposite is reported: the door of faith stood open to them.

questions: The crowd at Lystra swung from worship to stoning in a matter of days. Where are you tempted to build your confidence on people's approval rather than on God?

Paul met pagans with a word about the Creator's kindness in rain and harvest. Who in your life shares no faith background, and how might God's ordinary goodness become a bridge to the gospel with them?
The apostles tore their clothes rather than accept glory that belonged to God. What honour or credit are you holding onto that you should be handing back to God?
They taught that we enter the kingdom through many hardships. How does that sober word steady you when following Christ brings difficulty rather than ease?
They returned to strengthen the very churches born in hostile cities and appointed elders. Where is God calling you not just to start something but to stay and help it stand?

translationNotes.note: The crowd names Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, the chief speaker; in local legend Zeus and Hermes had once visited the region in disguise, which explains their eagerness to sacrifice.
Turn from these worthless things to the living God echoes the prophets' scorn for idols and Israel's confession of the one Creator, the standard shape of witness to pagans.
Appointed elders renders a verb that carried the sense of formal appointment; the apostles ordain local leadership in each church, entrusting them to the Lord with prayer and fasting.
